title: VI. For Awhile A Very Obscure One
paragraphs: After parting from Alyosha, Ivan headed home to Fyodor Pavlovitch's house. But, strange to say, he was overcome by an unbearable depression, which grew greater with every step he took toward the house. There was nothing strange about him being depressed; what was strange was that Ivan couldn't have said what was causing it. He had often been depressed before, and there was nothing surprising about him feeling that way at such a moment, when he had just broken with everything that had brought him here, and was preparing that very day to make a new start and enter on a new, unknown future. He would be solitary again, and though he had great hopes — and great, too great, expectations of life — he couldn't have given any definite account of his hopes, his expectations, or even his desires.

Yet at that moment, though apprehension of the new and unknown certainly had a place in his heart, what was worrying him was something quite different. “Is it loathing for my father's house?” he wondered. “Quite likely; I'm so sick of it; and though it's the last time I'll cross its hateful threshold, still I loathe it.... No, it isn't that either. Is it the parting with Alyosha and the conversation I had with him? For so many years I've been silent with the whole world and haven't deigned to speak, and all of a sudden I reel off a rigmarole like that.” It might well have been the youthful vexation of youthful inexperience and vanity — vexation at having failed to express himself, especially with a person like Alyosha, on whom his heart had certainly been counting. No doubt that came in, that vexation; it must have. But still, that wasn't it — that wasn't it either. “I feel sick with depression, and yet I can't tell what I want. Better not think, perhaps.”

Ivan tried “not to think,” but that was no use either. What made his depression so vexing and irritating was that it had a kind of casual, external character — he could feel it. Some person or thing seemed to be standing out somewhere, just the way something will sometimes obtrude itself on the eye, and though one may be so busy with work or conversation that for a long time one doesn't notice it, yet it irritates and almost torments one until at last one realizes what it is and removes the offending object — often quite a trifling and ridiculous one — some article left in the wrong place, a handkerchief on the floor, a book not returned to the shelf, and so on.
At last, feeling very cross and ill-humored, Ivan arrived home, and suddenly, about fifteen paces from the garden gate, he realized what had been fretting and worrying him.

On a bench by the gateway sat the valet Smerdyakov, enjoying the coolness of the evening, and at the first glance at him Ivan knew that it was the valet Smerdyakov who was on his mind, and that it was this man that his soul loathed. It all dawned on him suddenly and became clear. Just before, when Alyosha had been telling him about his meeting with Smerdyakov, he'd felt a sudden twinge of gloom and loathing that had immediately stirred answering anger in his heart. Later, as he talked, Smerdyakov had been forgotten for the time being; but he'd still been in his mind, and as soon as Ivan parted with Alyosha and was walking home, the forgotten sensation had begun to obtrude itself again. “Is it possible that a miserable, contemptible creature like that can worry me so much?” he wondered, with unbearable irritation.

It was true that lately Ivan had come to feel an intense dislike for the man, especially in the last few days. He had even begun to notice in himself a growing feeling that was almost like hatred for the creature. Perhaps this hatred was sharpened by the fact that when Ivan first arrived in the neighborhood he had felt quite differently. Then he had taken a marked interest in Smerdyakov, and had even thought him quite original. He'd encouraged him to talk to him, although he'd always been struck by a certain incoherence, or rather restlessness, in his mind, and couldn't understand what it was that so continually and insistently worked on the brain of ‘the contemplator.’ They discussed philosophical questions, and even how there could have been light on the first day when the sun, moon, and stars weren't created until the fourth day, and how that was to be understood. But Ivan soon saw that, though the sun, moon, and stars might be an interesting subject, to Smerdyakov they were quite secondary, and that he was looking for something altogether different. In one way and another, he began to betray a boundless vanity — and a wounded vanity at that — and Ivan didn't like it. It was what first gave rise to his aversion. Later there was trouble in the house. Grushenka had come onto the scene, and there were the scandals with his brother Dmitri — they discussed that, too. But though Smerdyakov always talked about that with great excitement, it was impossible to tell what he wanted to come of it. There was, in fact, something surprising in the illogicality and incoherence of some of his desires, accidentally let slip and always vaguely expressed. Smerdyakov was always inquiring, putting certain indirect but obviously premeditated questions — but what his object was he didn't explain, and usually at the most important moment he'd break off and relapse into silence, or switch to another subject. But what in the end most irritated Ivan and confirmed his dislike for him was the peculiar, revolting familiarity that Smerdyakov began to show more and more markedly. Not that he forgot himself and became rude; on the contrary, he always spoke very respectfully — and yet he had obviously begun to consider (goodness knows why!) that there was some sort of understanding between himself and Ivan Fyodorovitch. He always spoke in a tone suggesting that the two of them had some kind of compact, some secret between them, that had at some point been expressed on both sides, known only to them and beyond the comprehension of those around them. But for a long while Ivan didn't recognize the real cause of his growing dislike, and only lately had he realized what was at the root of it.

With a feeling of disgust and irritation he tried to pass through the gate without speaking or looking at Smerdyakov. But Smerdyakov rose from the bench, and from that action alone Ivan knew instantly that the man particularly wanted to talk to him. Ivan looked at him and stopped, and the fact that he did stop, instead of walking past as he'd intended to do only a minute before, drove him to fury. With anger and revulsion he looked at Smerdyakov's emasculate, sickly face, with the little curls combed forward on his forehead. His left eye winked and he grinned as if to say, “Where are you going? You're not going to walk past; you see that we two clever people have something to say to each other.”

Ivan shook. “Get away, miserable idiot. What have I got to do with you?” was on the tip of his tongue, but to his profound astonishment he heard himself say, “Is my father still asleep, or is he awake?”

He asked the question softly and meekly, to his own surprise, and at once, again to his own surprise, sat down on the bench. For an instant he felt almost frightened; he remembered it afterward. Smerdyakov stood facing him, his hands behind his back, looking at him with confidence and almost severity.

“His honor is still asleep,” he articulated deliberately (“You were the first to speak, not I,” he seemed to say). “I'm surprised at you, sir,” he added after a pause, lowering his eyes affectedly, setting his right foot forward, and playing with the tip of his polished boot.

“Why are you surprised at me?” Ivan asked abruptly and sullenly, doing his utmost to restrain himself, and realizing with disgust that he was feeling intense curiosity and wouldn't have gone away without satisfying it for anything.

“Why don't you go to Tchermashnya, sir?” Smerdyakov suddenly raised his eyes and smiled familiarly. “You must understand why I'm smiling for yourself, if you're a clever man,” his screwed-up left eye seemed to say.
“Why should I go to Tchermashnya?” Ivan asked in surprise.
Smerdyakov was silent again.

“Fyodor Pavlovitch himself has so begged you to,” he said at last, slowly and apparently attaching no significance to his answer. “I'm putting you off with a secondary reason,” he seemed to imply, “simply to say something.”
“Damn you! Speak out — what do you want!” Ivan cried angrily at last, passing from meekness to violence.
Smerdyakov drew his right foot up to his left, pulled himself up, but still looked at him with the same serenity and the same little smile.
“Nothing substantially — just by way of conversation.”

Another silence followed. They didn't speak for nearly a minute. Ivan knew he ought to get up and show anger, and Smerdyakov stood before him as if waiting to see whether he would be angry or not. So at least it seemed to Ivan. At last he moved to get up. Smerdyakov seemed to seize the moment.
“I'm in an awful position, Ivan Fyodorovitch. I don't know how to help myself,” he said resolutely and distinctly, and at his last word he sighed. Ivan Fyodorovitch sat back down.

“They are both utterly crazy — they're no better than little children,” Smerdyakov went on. “I'm speaking of your parent and your brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch. Any moment now, Fyodor Pavlovitch will get up and start worrying me every minute: ‘Has she come? Why hasn't she come?’ and so on until midnight and even after midnight. And if Agrafena Alexandrovna doesn't come (and very likely she doesn't mean to come at all), then he'll be at me again tomorrow morning: ‘Why hasn't she come? When will she come?’ — as though I'm to blame. On the other side it's no better. As soon as it gets dark, or even before, your brother will appear with his gun in his hands: ‘Look out, you rogue, you soup-maker — if you miss her and don't let me know she's been here, I'll kill you before anyone.’ When the night's over, in the morning, he too, like Fyodor Pavlovitch, starts worrying me to death: ‘Why hasn't she come? Will she come soon?’ And he, too, thinks I'm to blame because his lady hasn't come. Every day and every hour they grow angrier and angrier, so that sometimes I think I'll kill myself out of fright. I can't rely on them, sir.”
“And why have you meddled? Why did you start spying for Dmitri Fyodorovitch?” Ivan said irritably.

“How could I help meddling? Though, indeed, I haven't meddled at all, if you want to know the truth of the matter. I kept quiet from the very beginning, not daring to answer; but he fixed on me to be his servant. He's had only one thing to say, over and over: ‘I'll kill you, you scoundrel, if you miss her.’ I feel certain, sir, that I'll have a long fit tomorrow.”
“What do you mean by ‘a long fit’?”

“A long fit, lasting a long time — several hours, or perhaps a day or two. Once it went on for three days. I fell from the garret that time. The struggling stopped and then began again, and for three days I couldn't come back to my senses. Fyodor Pavlovitch sent for Herzenstube, the doctor here, and he put ice on my head and tried another remedy too.... I might have died.”
“But they say you can't tell with epilepsy when a fit is coming. What makes you say you'll have one tomorrow?” Ivan asked, with peculiar, irritable curiosity.
“That's just so. You can't tell beforehand.”
“Besides, you fell from the garret then.”
“I climb up to the garret every day. I might fall from the garret again tomorrow. And if not, I might fall down the cellar steps. I have to go into the cellar every day, too.”
Ivan took a long look at him.
“You're talking nonsense, I see, and I don't quite follow you,” he said softly, but with a sort of menace. “Are you planning to pretend to be ill tomorrow for three days, eh?”
Smerdyakov, who had lowered his eyes again and was playing with the toe of his right foot, set that foot down, moved the left one forward, and, grinning, articulated:

“If I were able to pull off such a trick — that is, pretend to have a fit — and it wouldn't be difficult for a man accustomed to them — I'd have a perfect right to use such a means to save myself from death. For even if Agrafena Alexandrovna comes to see his father while I'm ill, his honor can't blame a sick man for not telling him. He'd be ashamed to.”

“Hang it all!” Ivan cried, his face working with anger, “why are you always in such a funk for your life? All my brother Dmitri's threats are only hasty words and mean nothing. He won't kill you — it's not you he'll kill!”
“He'd kill me first of all, like a fly. But even more than that, I'm afraid I'd be taken for an accomplice of his when he does something crazy to his father.”
“Why should you be taken for an accomplice?”
“They'll think I'm an accomplice because I told him the signals as a great secret.”
“What signals? Whom did you tell? Confound you, speak more plainly.”

“I'm bound to admit it,” Smerdyakov drawled with pedantic composure, “that I have a secret with Fyodor Pavlovitch in this business. As you yourself know (if indeed you do know it), for several days past he's been locking himself in as soon as night, or even evening, comes on. Lately you've been going upstairs to your room early every evening, and yesterday you didn't come down at all, and so perhaps you don't know how carefully he's begun to lock himself in at night, and that even if Grigory Vassilyevitch comes to the door, he won't open to him until he hears his voice. But Grigory Vassilyevitch doesn't come, because I wait on him alone in his room now. That's the arrangement he made himself, ever since this to-do with Agrafena Alexandrovna began. But at night, by his orders, I go out to the lodge, so that I don't get to sleep until midnight but am on watch, getting up and walking about the yard, waiting for Agrafena Alexandrovna to come. For the last few days he's been perfectly frantic expecting her. What he argues is, she's afraid of him — Dmitri Fyodorovitch (Mitya, as he calls him) — ‘and so,’ says he, ‘she'll come the back way, late at night, to me. You keep watch for her,’ says he, ‘until midnight and later; and if she comes, you run up and knock at my door, or at the window from the garden. Knock first twice, rather gently, and then three times more quickly; then,’ says he, ‘I'll understand at once that she's come, and will open the door to you quietly.’ Another signal he gave me in case anything unexpected happens. At first, two knocks, and then, after an interval, another much louder. Then he'll understand that something has happened suddenly and that I have to see him, and he'll open to me so I can go in and speak to him. That's all in case Agrafena Alexandrovna can't come herself but sends a message. Besides, Dmitri Fyodorovitch might come too, so I have to let him know he's nearby. His honor is terribly afraid of Dmitri Fyodorovitch, so that even if Agrafena Alexandrovna had come and were locked in with him, and Dmitri Fyodorovitch were to turn up anywhere nearby at the time, I'd be bound to let him know at once, by knocking three times. So the first signal of five knocks means ‘Agrafena Alexandrovna has come,’ while the second signal of three knocks means ‘something important to tell you.’ His honor has shown me them several times and explained them. And since in the whole universe no one knows of these signals but myself and his honor, he'd open the door without the slightest hesitation and without calling out (he's terribly afraid of calling out aloud). Well, those signals are known to Dmitri Fyodorovitch too, now.”
“How are they known? Did you tell him? How dared you tell him?”

“It was out of fright I did it. How could I dare keep it back from him? Dmitri Fyodorovitch kept insisting every day, ‘You're deceiving me, you're hiding something from me! I'll break both your legs for you.’ So I told him those secret signals, so he might see my slavish devotion and be satisfied that I wasn't deceiving him, but was telling him everything I could.”
“If you think he'll make use of those signals and try to get in, don't let him in.”
“But if I'm laid up with a fit, how can I prevent him coming in, even if I dared prevent him, knowing how desperate he is?”
“Hang it! How can you be so sure you're going to have a fit, confound you? Are you laughing at me?”
“How would I dare laugh at you? I'm in no laughing mood, with this fear on me. I feel I'm going to have a fit. I have a presentiment. Fright alone will bring it on.”
“Confound it! If you're laid up, Grigory will be on watch. Tell Grigory beforehand; he'll be sure not to let him in.”

“I'd never dare tell Grigory Vassilyevitch about the signals without orders from my master. And as for Grigory Vassilyevitch hearing him and not admitting him — he's been ill since yesterday, and Marfa Ignatyevna plans to give him medicine tomorrow. They've just arranged it. It's a very peculiar remedy of hers. Marfa Ignatyevna knows of a preparation and always keeps some of it. It's a strong thing made from a certain herb. She has the secret of it, and she always gives it to Grigory Vassilyevitch three times a year when his lumbago is so bad it almost paralyzes him. Then she takes a towel, wets it with the stuff, and rubs his whole back for half an hour until it's red and swollen, and what's left in the bottle she gives him to drink with a special prayer — but not quite all, for on such occasions she leaves some for herself, and drinks it herself. And since they never take strong drink, I assure you they both drop asleep at once and sleep soundly for a very long time. When Grigory Vassilyevitch wakes up he's perfectly well after it, but Marfa Ignatyevna always has a headache. So if Marfa Ignatyevna carries out her intention tomorrow, they won't hear anything and won't hinder Dmitri Fyodorovitch. They'll be asleep.”

“What a rigmarole! And it all seems to happen at once, as though it were planned. You'll have a fit and they'll both be unconscious,” Ivan cried. “Aren't you trying to arrange it so?” suddenly broke from him, and he frowned menacingly.
“How could I?... And why should I, when it all depends on Dmitri Fyodorovitch and his plans?... If he means to do something, he'll do it; but if not, I'm not going to push him onto his father.”

“And why would he go to father — especially on the sly — if, as you say yourself, Agrafena Alexandrovna won't come at all?” Ivan went on, turning white with anger. “You say that yourself, and the whole time I've been here I've been sure it was all the old man's fantasy, and that the creature won't come to him. Why should Dmitri break in on him if she doesn't come? Speak — I want to know what you're thinking!”

“You know yourself why he'll come. What's the use of what I think? His honor will come simply because he's in a rage, or suspicious perhaps on account of my illness, and he'll dash in, as he did yesterday, through impatience to search the rooms to see whether she hasn't slipped in on the sly. He's perfectly well aware, too, that Fyodor Pavlovitch has a big envelope with three thousand roubles in it, tied up with ribbon and sealed with three seals. On it is written in his own hand, ‘To my angel Grushenka, if she'll come,’ to which he added three days later, ‘for my little chicken.’ There's no telling what that might do.”

“Nonsense!” Ivan cried, almost beside himself. “Dmitri won't come to steal money and kill my father to do it. He might have killed him yesterday on account of Grushenka, like the frantic, savage fool he is, but he won't steal.”

“He's in very great need of money now — the greatest need, Ivan Fyodorovitch. You don't know how much need he's in,” Smerdyakov explained with perfect composure and remarkable distinctness. “He looks on that three thousand as his own, too. He said so to me himself. ‘My father still owes me three thousand,’ he said. And besides that, consider, Ivan Fyodorovitch — there's something else perfectly true. It's as good as certain, so to speak, that Agrafena Alexandrovna will force him, if she only wants to, to marry her — the master himself, I mean, Fyodor Pavlovitch — if she only wants to, and of course she may want to. All I've said is that she won't come, but maybe she's looking for more than that — I mean, to be mistress here. I know myself that Samsonov, her merchant, was laughing with her about it, telling her quite openly that it wouldn't be at all a stupid thing to do. And she's got plenty of sense. She wouldn't marry a beggar like Dmitri Fyodorovitch. So, taking that into consideration, Ivan Fyodorovitch, reflect that then neither Dmitri Fyodorovitch nor yourself, nor your brother, Alexey Fyodorovitch, would have anything after the master's death — not a rouble — because Agrafena Alexandrovna would marry him simply to get hold of it all, all the money there is. But if your father were to die now, there'd be some forty thousand for sure, even for Dmitri Fyodorovitch, whom he hates so — because he's made no will.... Dmitri Fyodorovitch knows all that very well.”
A sort of shudder passed over Ivan's face. He suddenly flushed.

“Then why on earth,” he suddenly interrupted Smerdyakov, “do you advise me to go to Tchermashnya? What did you mean by that? If I go away, you see what will happen here.” Ivan drew his breath with difficulty.
“Precisely so,” Smerdyakov said, softly and reasonably, watching Ivan intently all the while.
“What do you mean by ‘precisely so’?” Ivan questioned him, with a menacing light in his eyes, restraining himself with difficulty.

“I spoke because I felt sorry for you. If I were in your place, I'd simply throw it all up ... rather than stay on in such a position,” Smerdyakov answered, with the most candid air, looking at Ivan's flashing eyes. They were both silent.

“You seem to be a perfect idiot, and what's more ... an awful scoundrel, too.” Ivan rose abruptly from the bench. He was about to pass straight through the gate, but he stopped short and turned to Smerdyakov. Something strange followed. In a sudden paroxysm, Ivan bit his lip, clenched his fists, and in another moment would have flung himself on Smerdyakov. The latter, at any rate, noticed it at the same moment, started, and shrank back. But the moment passed without harm to Smerdyakov, and Ivan turned in silence, in what seemed like perplexity, to the gate.
“I'm going away to Moscow tomorrow, if you care to know — early tomorrow morning. That's all!” he suddenly said aloud, angrily, and wondered afterward what need there was to say that to Smerdyakov.
“That's the best thing you can do,” Smerdyakov answered, as though he'd expected to hear it; “except that you can always be telegraphed for from Moscow, if anything should happen here.”

Ivan stopped again, and again turned quickly to Smerdyakov. But a change had passed over him, too. All his familiarity and carelessness had completely vanished. His face expressed attention and expectation, intent but timid and cringing.
“Haven't you something more to say — something to add?” could be read in the intent gaze he fixed on Ivan.
“And couldn't I be sent for from Tchermashnya, too — in case anything happens?” Ivan shouted suddenly, for some unknown reason raising his voice.
“From Tchermashnya, too ... you could be sent for,” Smerdyakov muttered, almost in a whisper, looking disconcerted, but gazing intently into Ivan's eyes.
“Only Moscow is farther and Tchermashnya is nearer. Is it to save me spending money on the fare, or to save me going so far out of my way, that you insist on Tchermashnya?”

“Precisely so...” Smerdyakov muttered, with a breaking voice. He looked at Ivan with a revolting smile, and again made ready to draw back. But to his astonishment Ivan broke into a laugh, and went through the gate still laughing. Anyone who had seen his face at that moment would have known that he wasn't laughing from lightness of heart, and he himself couldn't have explained what he was feeling at that instant. He moved and walked as though in a nervous frenzy.
